ITU Copenhagen · Autumn 2026 · Thursdays

Technical Interaction Design / Weekly Syllabus

In the first six weeks each of you builds and deploys a working app of your own; the group app starts after the autumn break, on what you have each already built. At the same time, a design track focuses on understanding users, designing for them, and improving the design.

  • Every team builds the same basic to-do app, but adds their own feature for a specific group of users.
  • Each week includes a lecture, a two-hour exercise, and a project milestone.
  • Use the basic app yourself, design the new feature for people different from you, and be able to explain all your code at the exam.
  • Hand-ins are due on a Tuesday, at the time learnIT gives for each.

Before week 1, you only need to complete JavaScript, the Language. The other TopUps are introduced later, just before you need them.

In the AI era, the important skill is understanding code, not just writing it. You can use AI as much as you want, but you must understand and explain every line of code at the exam. The course is designed around this idea.

Week 01
Aug 27
MirceaLecture · React I + opening
First React app: components and props
After the opening — what the course is, and the deal about AI: use it as much as you like, and own every line at the exam — React, built live on a tiny to-do app: React as a library rather than a framework, everything a component, JSX and its rules (one root, closed tags, className), curly-brace interpolation, props and destructuring, children, rendering a list with map and keys, and onClick — passing a function rather than calling it. State did not fit and moved to week 2.

Week 02
Sep 3
MirceaLecture · React II
State, forms, lists, and local storage
Week 1's leftover first: state. Props are read-only by promise, not by enforcement — pushing onto one worked, live. Then useState, React as a spreadsheet that recomputes, and the two rules that make a re-render happen: call the setter, and pass it a new array rather than the same one changed. Then the to-do became a real app: a controlled form for adding, a callback from the form to the list, items as objects with ids, delete and check-off, and two components pulled out because they were wanted twice — TextInput and TodoItem. It ended with conditional rendering, and useEffect keeping the list in local storage, so it survives a refresh. The class voted to run twenty minutes over rather than lose the end.
Exercise · 2h solo
first hourCopy the class code into week-02/. Add useState for the to-dos and a controlled form that adds to them; turn the strings into objects with ids; give each a checkbox and a Delete button.
second hourStill individual: an empty-list message, then save the list to local storage with useEffect and load it back with useState(loadTodos).

Week 04
Sep 17
MirceaLecture · Backend I
Replacing local storage with a real database
Parse and Back4App: setting up a backend, and the to-do list you already have re-implemented on top of it — create with save(), read with a Parse.Query and await, update a single field, and delete, all of it in one file to begin with. The objectId became the React key. Answering a question about what an API is took a detour through HTTP and REST, a live curl, and what an SDK adds on top of them. The bugs that came up along the way were fixed in front of the room: a list that was not an array, and fields that need get().

Week 05
Sep 24
MirceaLecture · Backend II
Authentication, authorization, and the first relationship
Two words that sound alike and mean different things. Authentication: signup and login, Parse.User.current(), and the app gated on it with the conditional rendering from week 2; the session token in local storage, and what someone who steals it can do. Authorization, in layers: an ACL on each object, owner-only and then shared; class-level permissions; and why hiding a button is not security, shown by a curl that walks straight past the UI. Roles were explained but not demonstrated, and Parse has no field-level permissions, so a private field means a separate table. Then the first relationship: every item points to its owner, and then to a List — one-to-many, a pointer as a foreign key.
Exercise
1h soloAdd an auth page and conditional rendering to your own app; give each item an owner pointer; lock the class to logged-in users; show only your own items; log out and try another user. Further: real ACLs, an authService.js, a role.
1h projectThe user study, written up.

Week 06
Oct 1
MirceaLecture · Backend III + routing + deploy
Sharing a list, going live, and routing

Week 5's leftover first: sharing a list is a many-to-many relationship between users and lists, so it gets a join table of its own, ListMember, with the ACLs that follow from it — and what leaving a list does and does not undo. Then the app went public: npm run build, GitHub Pages, and the Back4App keys sitting in plain sight in the bundle, which is fine only because the ACLs are doing their job. Then routing: why a single-page app still needs URLs, React Router with a page per list (/lists/:listId), links, and why a URL is not a permission. Refreshing a route on GitHub Pages gives a 404, and copying index.html to 404.html fixes it.

The group app was meant to start this week. It starts after the break instead: every member first builds sharing and routing alone, in their own app.

Exercise
1h soloIn your own app, load the user's lists, give each its own form and its own to-dos through a pointer, then give each list its own page with React Router and Link.
1h projectDeploy your own app to GitHub Pages and make refresh work.

Week 07
Oct 8
KonstantinaLecture · Design IIMircea away
Screens, and judging them: wireframing & usability
Opened with feedback on the user studies: focus on what users have to do, not on features; tie each task to what an interview said; keep the core small; transcripts go in the appendix. Then from a user story to the screens: functional requirements (what the app must do) and non-functional ones (how it should feel: usable, accessible, quick, clear about errors), a user flow, and the wireframe — the structural skeleton, low fidelity on purpose, because a rough sketch is cheap to change and says "this is still open". Wireframes need states, not just the happy path: empty, error, saving, success. And how to test one: a think-aloud, without leading the participant, watching for hesitation, mistakes and wrong expectations, then change and test again.
Exercise
1h soloFigma, with Lea: a team with Education status, frames, auto layout, components, dev mode, and the community files.

Week 10
Nov 5
MirceaLecture · Code organisation II
Where the state goes: extraction and lifting

The check-in week, so the lecture is a refactor of code you already have rather than a mechanism you have never seen — the exercise slot is spent talking about your own app, which is the wrong place to meet a new API and the right place to meet a new standard.

Since week 8 the review checklist has said state where it belongs without anything ever saying where that is. This is where. Extracting components first, because extraction is what creates the problem: split one screen into three and two of them need to agree about state that now belongs to neither, which is lifting state up. Then useRef, for the two or three things state cannot do. The worked example is the one that bites in week 12 — stopping a task in one list when another starts in a different one.

Exercise · 2h studio
at homeExtract one overgrown component in your own repo, and lift whatever state the extraction stranded. Do it before Thursday — the slot itself is a studio.
2h studioEveryone in the room refactoring their own app, while Mircea and a TA each run five 20-minute check-ins on the extended data model and what is actually built. Bring the ER diagram on one page — we have had it since 27 Oct, so the twenty minutes are for the awkward parts, not the summary.

Week 11
Nov 12
MirceaLecture · Backend III
Talking to the backend well

One subject in three moves, all of it about the wire between your app and Parse. Do less over it: fewer round trips, fetch what you will actually use. Then move work across it, into cloud functions, where it belongs server-side. Then stop asking altogether — live queries, push instead of poll, and the shared list that updates itself while somebody else is typing into it. Two people on one task is where multi-user reality lands on an app you have been using for weeks, and it sets up the collision week 12 has to resolve: if two people track time on the same task, whose time is it?

Examples stay in JavaScript. TypeScript is permitted if a whole group agrees and already has the experience — never as a second track.

Exercise
1h soloWrite one cloud function and measure the round-trips saved; subscribe to a live query and react to a remote change.
1h projectMove one operation server-side; put live sync on a shared list.

Week 12
Nov 19
KonstantinaLecture · Feature depthMircea away
Time-tracking, and the idea of context
Opens with feedback on the accessibility audits and visual passes handed in nine days ago. Then: a simple feature that blooms. You cannot run two timers at once, so starting one must stop another — which means the app has to know what is active. That is a context spanning every list, and it is the first thing in the course that is genuinely awkward to hold in your head. Since Parse ACLs are object-level and not field-level, private timing splits into its own table. This is where AI stops being much help, which is rather the point.
Exercise
1h soloBuild a start/stop timer with a single active context.
1h projectTeams who chose it: add time-tracking with context. Everyone else — and everyone, if week 9 ran out of hour: the responsive pass, breakpoints included.

How the pieces fit

The exercise slot

1h solo, then 1h project — from week 3 onward. Weeks 1 and 2 are two hours of your own work, because there are no teams yet. Solo drills are required but ungraded — an existence check, not a grading anvil — and they pile up into a personal portfolio that is your exam prep. On the design weeks (3, 7 and 9) the solo hour drills that week's own skill; a couple of times in the back half it swaps "build X" for "review this AI-generated PR on your repo and write three comments you'd defend."

Two repos, two jobs

A shared reference to-do, git-tagged per lecture, is the canonical good code, and it is for reading rather than for starting from. Teams build their own repo from empty in week 6. They have the wiring already — each member set up a Parse app alone in weeks 4 and 5 — and their data model is the ER diagram they argued from their own tasks, so what a copy of the reference would give them is a to-do list they would then have to unpick. Starting empty is also what makes the user study decide the app rather than decorate it — after the user study has said what they are building, and after every member has stood up a backend alone. A personal exercise repo — one folder per week, week-01/ through week-14/, public — holds the solo drills, checked at a glance rather than by pull request. Both URLs are collected in week 1 and week 6, which is what makes checking at a glance possible at all.

The project constraint

Lean required core: owner → lists → items, sharing at the list level. Everything else is an optional feature menu — project grouping, time-tracking with context, two people on one task — that teams pick from and defend. One population, one twist, fully built.

Feedback without pull requests

No weekly PR reviews; they never scaled at this size. What replaced them works on six group artefacts rather than twenty-five individual ones, and it is spoken rather than written: ten minutes at the start of a lecture, across all groups at once, so everybody hears what everybody else got wrong. Around it: dogfooding tells you continuously whether the thing works, AI is your always-on first-pass code reviewer, and two sit-down conversations per group land in weeks 10.

A pulse, every week

The last two minutes of every lecture: an anonymous single-box form, the same link every week, one question. Read before the next lecture and reported back at the start of it — that second half is what makes students keep filling it in. Fourteen cheap readings beat one end-of-term survey you can no longer act on.

Assessment

70% individual exam, 30% group project, with a hard floor: bomb the individual and you fail, however strong the group. The project is your exam curriculum — if you used it, you understand it.

Pre-course

**JavaScript, the Language is the one module required before week 1, with Scrimba's free tier as the interactive companion (Learn JavaScript, 9.4h, MDN-built; Learn HTML & CSS 5.7h and Learn React 15.1h as bonuses). A Node/npm setup step** runs pre-course. The remaining TopUps arrive on the card of the week they serve.
